steps.body: A random sample lets you estimate the WHOLE population without asking everyone. If 30 of 50 sampled students like pizza, that's 3/5 — scale that same ratio up to the full school.
Scale a sample up to the population.

predict.prompt: 30 of 50 sampled students prefer pizza. The school has 500 students — ten times the sample. What should the estimate be?

options.label: Still 30 — the sample already counted them
250 — half the school, since 30 is about half the sample

predict.reveal: A sample estimate assumes the same RATIO holds in the whole population. 500 is ten times 50, so the count scales by ten as well: 300. The ratio stays fixed while both numbers grow — which is what the table will show.

widget.prompt: The sample is 30 out of 50. Fill in the row for the whole school of 500, keeping the ratio the same.
widget.successFeedback: 300. Look down the column: 30 out of 50, 60 out of 100, 300 out of 500 — the ratio never changed, only the size of the group. That constant ratio IS the assumption a sample estimate rests on.
widget.lowFeedback: Too low. 500 is ten times the 50 you sampled, so the count has to grow by the same factor — compare your row against the ones above it.
widget.highFeedback: Too high — that is more than the ratio allows. 30 out of every 50 is well under everyone; scaling it to 500 cannot exceed 300.

explanationVariants: Scale the sample's ratio up to the full population.

widget.prompt: In a sample of 40 people, 12 own a bike. If the town has 200 people, estimate how many own a bike.

commonErrors.feedback: That's just the sample count. Scale it up: 12/40 of 200 = 60.
That's the whole town, not just bike owners. Scale the ratio: 60.

steps.body: A sample must be RANDOM to give a fair estimate — asking only your friends, or only people at one club meeting, skews the result toward that group.

widget.prompt: A school wants to know if students like math class. Which sampling method gives the LEAST biased estimate?

options.label: Randomly select 50 students from the full enrollment list
options.feedback: Yes — a random selection from everyone gives every student an equal chance, avoiding bias.

options.label: Ask the 50 students in the math club
options.feedback: Math club members are far more likely to enjoy math class — this sample is biased toward liking it.

options.label: Ask the first 50 students who arrive early
options.feedback: Early arrivers might share other traits unrelated to random chance — not a fair, random sample.

steps.body: A bigger, truly random sample usually gives a more reliable estimate than a small one — but even a modest random sample beats a large biased one.

widget.prompt: In a sample of 25 people, 7 prefer tea over coffee. If the office has 300 people, estimate how many prefer tea.

commonErrors.feedback: That's just the sample count. Scale it up: 7/25 of 300 = 84.
That's the whole office, not just tea-drinkers. Scale the ratio: 84.

explanationVariants: A random selection from the whole list avoids bias toward any one group.
Convenience samples (easiest to reach) tend to skew results.

widget.prompt: A city wants to know how residents feel about a new park. Which method is LEAST biased?

options.label: Randomly call 200 residents from the full city directory
options.feedback: Yes — a random call list gives every resident an equal chance of being included.

options.label: Survey people already AT the park
options.feedback: People at the park likely already like parks — this sample is biased in favor.

options.label: Post a survey only on the parks department's social media
options.feedback: Only parks-department followers would see it — a biased, non-random group.

explanationVariants: Scale the sample's ratio up to the full population.

widget.prompt: In a sample of 60 students, 18 walk to school. If the district has 480 students, estimate how many walk to school.

commonErrors.feedback: That's just the sample count. Scale it up: 18/60 of 480 = 144.
That's the whole district, not just walkers. Scale the ratio: 144.

explanationVariants: Scale the sample's ratio up to the full population.

widget.prompt: In a sample of 30 shoppers, 9 use reusable bags. If the store sees 900 shoppers a week, estimate how many use reusable bags.

commonErrors.feedback: That's just the sample count. Scale it up: 9/30 of 900 = 270.
That's all shoppers, not just reusable-bag users. Scale the ratio: 270.

hints: Find the sample's ratio: 9 out of 30 = 3/10.
Apply that same ratio to 900: 3/10 of 900.

steps.body: Scale a random sample's ratio up to estimate the whole population — but only if the sample was truly random, not biased toward one group.
takeaways: Estimate = (trait count in sample ÷ sample size) × population size.
A random sample gives every member an equal chance of being chosen.
A biased sample (friends, convenience, self-selected) skews the estimate.

concept.body: Scale a sample's ratio up to the whole population: (trait count ÷ sample size) × population size. 30 of 50 sampled (3/5) scales to 3/5 of 500 = 300.

explanationVariants: Scale the sample's ratio up to the population.
